synthesis.headline: A blocked western-trough/eastern-ridge omega pattern locks in Northeast heat while the Southwest monsoon and a Texas thermal low keep the water running
synthesis.narrative:
Today's continent is organized by a strongly blocked, amplified upper pattern: a towering longwave ridge over the Northeast and Atlantic Canada (500 mb heights into the 5800 dam range) opposite a broad, nearly stationary trough over the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, with a weak central-tier trough between them giving the CONUS a classic omega-like look. That single configuration explains nearly everything else on the map. Beneath the eastern ridge, dangerous heat is building from the Northern Plains through the Great Lakes and into the northern Mid-Atlantic, where triple digits are expected today into Thursday under Extreme Heat Warnings and Advisories. The western trough and its stratospheric dry intrusion — vividly red on the Air Mass RGB from the northern Rockies down through the Plains into northern Mexico — mark the sharp airmass boundary and jet axis that separates that dry, high-PV air from the moist green tropical airmass pressing north over the eastern half of the country.

The wettest, most dangerous focal point is the southern tier. A weak surface low and a warm-core 500 mb thermal feature over central Texas, anchored beneath a stationary Southern Plains-to-Southeast front, are driving repeated rounds of convection and significant flash-flood potential in the Texas Hill Country, where 6-8 inches with locally 10-plus inches are possible. This is a training/heavy-rain story more than a severe-wind story. The Southwest monsoon is the other engine: onshore, moisture-rich flow and the thermal-low complex over Arizona and New Mexico are focusing late-day terrain-driven storms across the interior West. The Canadian side of the ledger deserves equal billing — the full-disk imagery shows a deep, cold-core cyclone wrapping high-PV air near Hudson Bay, and the CMC surface analysis places sub-995 hPa lows over the Yukon border and Northwest Territories, trailing fronts into the Prairies against a robust 1033-1034 hPa high. It is the eastern-Canadian cyclone that is delivering the cold front now approaching the U.S. border, with a second front due Friday.

Upper-level context ties it together and tells us what happens next. The jet streak running from the central Plains northeastward into the Great Lakes and off New England, on the equatorward flank of the ridge, is where the modest severe threat lives today, while the blocked ridge guarantees the heat persists rather than mixing out. The WPC extended guidance keeps the ridge entrenched through the weekend, then nudges a shortwave around its northern flank into the Upper Midwest early next week, deepening the eastern trough, shunting the ridge axis west into the Intermountain West, and finally shifting the heat southward toward the Lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast. Monsoon moisture and repeated eastern-U.S. thunderstorm rounds continue throughout, so this is a slow, incremental pattern shift, not a clean break.
synthesis.climate_context: Seasonally this is peak North American Monsoon and mid-summer heat/severe season, and today's map is textbook for it: a thermal-low complex over the Southwest, deep Gulf moisture feeding the southern tier, and heat domes under amplified ridging. On the tropical side, the eastern Pacific is the busy basin — Tropical Storm Elida south of Baja, an 80% development area forecast south of Mexico, and additional disturbances near Hawaii — while the Atlantic is quieter, with only a low (around 20% over seven days) expected to form this weekend in the northeastern Gulf and drift toward the Florida Big Bend/Southeast coast; the WPC extended guidance flags growing model support for that Gulf low. The ENSO backdrop is a notable transition: weak La Niña that persisted through early 2026 has given way to neutral in spring and is now trending decisively toward El Niño, with the AMJ 2026 ONI already near +0.98, a developing warm episode that will increasingly shape the second half of hurricane season.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no mesoscale discussions active and is monitoring no organized convective threat at this hour. The Day 1 outlook is a patchwork of low-end Marginal risks: possible supercells for large hail/wind in the Mid-Atlantic (initiation uncertain, partly due to upstream wildfire smoke), low-topped damaging-wind storms in northern New England, terrain-driven storms in the northern Rockies/High Plains, orographic and monsoon storms in the Pacific Northwest and Arizona, and — notably — a brief tornado threat in south-central Texas where a weak mid-level low overlaps very moist low-level air and up to 100 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH. The overriding regional hazard, however, remains life-threatening flash flooding in the Texas Hill Country.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The pattern is dominated by a strong 1025 mb high centered over the central Plains, with a secondary high near 1024 mb positioned over the upper Midwest and another high around 1021 mb off the Atlantic Seaboard. A cluster of lows is evident across the Southwest and southern Rockies, with central pressures reading near 1013 mb over New Mexico and 1020 mb over Arizona, consistent with the thermal low complex typical of summer monsoon season. A cold front extends from the northern Plains southward through the central Plains, with a warm front draped across the upper Great Lakes region, and what appears to be a stationary boundary near the Gulf Coast interacting with onshore moisture flow from the Gulf of Mexico. Pressure gradients are tightest along the Pacific Northwest coast where isobars are closely packed around the 1021 mb high over the interior Northwest, while gradients are quite slack across the Southeast under the sprawling Bermuda high. The primary moisture focus is across the southern Plains and Gulf Coast, where the frontal boundary and weak low near 1018 mb over Texas are drawing Gulf moisture northward, and the monsoon flow into the Southwest is concentrating lift along the terrain of Arizona and New Mexico.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: Valid 0000Z 15 July 2026, the CMC surface analysis shows a pair of lows anchoring the Canadian pattern: a 991 hPa low over the Yukon-Alaska border and a 992 hPa system over the central Northwest Territories, both trailing frontal boundaries southeastward into the Prairies and connecting to a broader trough extending toward the northern Great Plains of the United States. A strong 1027 hPa high over the British Columbia-Alberta border and a 1034-1033 hPa high complex across the central Prairies into Saskatchewan create a tight pressure gradient along their northern flanks, suggesting brisk surface winds across Alberta and Saskatchewan between the highs and the retreating frontal zone. Across Ontario and Quebec, a weak 1010-1019 hPa ridge provides relatively benign conditions, though a slow-moving frontal boundary draped near the Great Lakes region connects southward into an active area of low pressure and multiple fronts over the north-central United States, keeping the potential for lift and moisture advection near the border. Along the Pacific coast, the ridge dominates from coastal BC southward, limiting frontal activity there. The most active zone for precipitation and wind in Canada on this chart appears focused over the Northwest Territories trough corridor and the Prairie frontal boundary where gradient tightening is most pronounced.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 15 July 2026, the dominant feature is a highly amplified longwave ridge centered over the northeastern US and Atlantic Canada, with 500 mb heights reaching into the 5800 dam range and a pronounced thermal anomaly indicated by the deep red temperature shading across the Mid-Atlantic and New England. A broad longwave trough occupies the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, with heights in the 532-538 dam range across the Intermountain West, giving the overall pattern a classic western trough/eastern ridge configuration. A thermal low or cutoff-like feature is analyzed over central Texas near the Gulf Coast, showing slightly anomalous height falls in the 589 dam range but without strong closed contours visible, suggesting a warm-core 500 mb low more consistent with a thermal cyclone than a cold-core cutoff. The jet streak is clearly defined and oriented from the central Plains northeastward into the Great Lakes and off the New England coast, with wind speeds reaching 65-70 knots or greater on the equatorward flank of the ridge, placing the right entrance region over the Upper Midwest. The overall pattern is strongly blocked given the ridge amplification over the Northeast, favoring persistent anomalous heat there while the western trough remains nearly stationary.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
Valid 15 Jul 2026 16:41Z GOES-19 AirMass RGB.

A pronounced stratospheric dry intrusion dominates the western third of the image, with deep red and orange tones extending from the northern Rockies southward through the Great Plains into western Texas and northern Mexico, indicating high potential vorticity air descending from the stratosphere across that corridor. The implied jet axis runs along the sharp airmass boundary separating this orange-red air from the moist green airmass to the east, oriented roughly from the northern Plains southwestward into the Desert Southwest, consistent with a positively tilted upper trough or longwave ridge-trough couplet. No well-defined cutoff low is apparent, but the elongated PV streamer wrapping cyclonically into the central Plains near Kansas and Oklahoma suggests active upper-level dynamics there. Organized deep convection is evident over the Yucatan Peninsula and adjacent western Caribbean, where bright white cold tops punctuate a broad shield of moist tropical air, and a secondary cluster of convective towers is visible over central Texas near the dryline. The southeastern US and Gulf Coast remain firmly in warm moist tropical airmass with no significant organized convection visible at this hour.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
GOES-19 Air Mass RGB, 15 Jul 2026 16:30Z

A prominent cyclonic circulation is evident over the Canadian Arctic near Hudson Bay, outlined by the classic orange-red hues of stratospheric-origin, high potential vorticity air wrapping into its core, indicating a deep cold-core system drawing down polar air. The polar jet boundary is sharply defined across central Canada, with a stark transition from the reddish-orange high-PV airmass to the moist green tropical air pressing northward across the central and eastern United States. Over the eastern Pacific west of Mexico and Central America, several clusters of bright white convective towers mark active deep convection along the ITCZ, with one particularly robust cell near 15N 110W suggesting a disturbance worth monitoring. The Caribbean and western Atlantic basin appear largely free of organized deep convection, with only isolated towers visible near Cuba and Hispaniola embedded in the moist tropical airmass. In the Southern Hemisphere, a vigorous extratropical cyclone is apparent near the Patagonian coast around 50S, with a well-defined warm-cold frontal structure curving into the south Atlantic, shown by the cloud-banded white and purple signatures extending northeast toward Uruguay.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking warm signal covers the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, where probabilities reach 80-90 percent above normal across Washington, Oregon, and Idaho, strongly suggesting a persistent upper-level ridge anchored over the West Coast through July 20-24. A second, nearly as intense above-normal signal occupies the Southeast, particularly Florida and the Gulf Coast states, where 70-80 percent probabilities indicate anomalous warmth likely tied to a separate subtropical high or suppressed convection. The central tier from the Dakotas through Nebraska and into the southern Rockies sits in a near-normal to slightly below-normal zone, implying a trough axis or relatively weak flow in between the two ridges that limits temperature extremes there. New England, the Great Lakes, and portions of the Northern Plains show 50-60 percent probabilities of below-normal temperatures, consistent with troughing persisting over the Northeast quadrant of the country. The overall pattern of a western ridge, central trough, and southeastern warmth is a classic amplified omega-like configuration that the model guidance projects to remain entrenched rather than break down, with no meaningful transition signal visible across the CONUS domain on this chart.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Strong upper-level high nearly stationary over northern tier, building southeast toward East Coast. Prolonged heat and humidity across Northern Plains to Great Lakes with highs in 90s-lower 100s; triple digits expected in northern Mid-Atlantic today/Thursday. Extreme Heat Warnings in Northern Plains, Heat Advisories across Great Lakes and portions of New England. Cold front from deepening eastern Canadian cyclone brings cooler air to U.S.-Canadian border; second front arrives Friday. Severe thunderstorms possible early Wednesday across northern New England and Montana; strong storms return Thursday in New England. Slow-moving pattern over southern tier with stationary front from Southern Plains to Southeast producing repeated thunderstorm rounds. Significant heavy rainfall continuing Texas Hill Country—6-8 inches with locally 10+ inches possible, dangerous flash flooding likely. Monsoonal moisture driving late-day/early-evening thunderstorms across interior West.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
MARGINAL RISK issued for severe thunderstorms across Mid-Atlantic, Northern New England, Northern Rockies/High Plains, Pacific Northwest, Arizona, and South-Central Texas through 16 December 1200Z.

Mid-Atlantic: Moderately unstable airmass (MLCAPE 1500-2500) south of frontal boundary with 40-50+ kt effective shear supporting supercells capable of large hail and damaging winds, but convective initiation highly uncertain due to marginal forcing location and upstream wildfire smoke.

Northern New England: Low-topped convection likely in strongest mid-level forcing with locally damaging wind gusts possible given unidirectional westerly winds and 30-40 kt low-level flow.

Northern Rockies/High Plains: Weak mid-level vorticity maximum moving northeast may trigger scattered afternoon storms with potential upscale growth and isolated severe wind gusts, though deep-layer shear remains modest.

Pacific Northwest: Isolated-scattered orographic thunderstorms east of Cascades with weak instability; isolated severe gusts possible in stronger cores.

Arizona: Weak to moderate instability from daytime heating supports isolated severe gusts initially over elevated terrain spreading westward.

South-Central Texas: Weak mid-level low may support brief tornadoes with ongoing convection given up to 100 m2/s2 0-1 km SRH and very moist low-level airmass.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions currently issued. No organized convective threat is actively being monitored by the Storm Prediction Center.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: Low pressure expected to form this weekend in the northeastern Gulf of America with slow northeastward movement. Development chances low through 48 hours (near 0%), increasing to 20% through seven days as the system moves toward the southeastern U.S. coast by early next week.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Elida recently upgraded, located south of Baja California. A trough southwest of Hawaii shows medium development potential (50% in 48 hours, 60% by day 7), could become depression by week's end. A second low south-southeast of Hawaii has decreasing development chances (20%). An area of low pressure expected to develop south of Mexico this week with high likelihood (80%) of tropical depression formation by weekend into early next week.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows weak La Niña conditions currently (SON 2025, anomaly -0.51), persisting through early 2026 with anomalies around -0.5 to -0.37. The phase transitions toward neutral in spring 2026 (JFM, anomaly -0.14), then shifts decisively toward El Niño by mid-year 2026. AMJ 2026 shows strong warming with anomaly +0.98, suggesting a developing warm episode. The trend indicates La Niña conditions weakening and dissipating as warmer waters establish themselves.
